headline: California exempts Linux from age-verification law
summary: Open-source operating systems like Linux and SteamOS are now exempt from California's upcoming Digital Age Assurance Act, thanks to a unanimous legislative vote.
details: California lawmakers have unanimously passed Assembly Bill 1856, exempting open-source operating systems from the Digital Age Assurance Act, which is set to take effect in January 2027. This amendment ensures that Linux distributions and SteamOS will not be required to collect user age data during account setup.

The bill redefines "operating system provider" to exclude entities distributing software under licenses like GPL, MIT, BSD, and Apache, which permit modification and redistribution. This carve-out specifically removes Debian, Fedora, Ubuntu, Arch, and BSD-based systems from the law's scope.

Further exclusions cover software components not offered as standalone applications, such as libraries and dependencies distributed via package managers like apt and pacman. Browser extension stores are also out of scope under a third carve-out.

The amendments also corrected a flawed definition of "user" that technically classified all device owners in California as children, preventing any user from being flagged as an adult. A new provision now prohibits requesting age signals unless legally required, closing potential data collection loopholes.

While Windows, macOS, iOS, and Android remain under the law's purview, requiring age collection at account setup, the status of SteamOS is still uncertain due to its distribution alongside the proprietary Steam client. GrapheneOS, previously vowing non-compliance, is now fully outside the law's scope.

Assemblymember Buffy Wicks, the author of both the original act and the amendment, introduced the exemption following criticism from Linux developers and the Electronic Frontier Foundation, aiming to protect open-source software from burdensome regulations.
